title: New Testament Survey: The Good News of Jesus
description: Journey through the entire New Testament, the four Gospels, the birth of the Church in Acts, the letters of Paul and others, and the hope of Revelation, and meet Jesus, the Savior of the world.
outcomes: Understand the structure and storyline of all 27 New Testament books
Know the life, teaching, death, and resurrection of Jesus from the four Gospels
Explain the gospel and how a person is saved
Trace the birth and growth of the early Church in Acts
Understand the main themes of Paul's and the general letters
Grasp the hope of Revelation and how the whole Bible fits together
requirements: A Bible (print or app) is helpful

faqs.question: Do I need to have read the New Testament before taking this?
faqs.answer: No. This survey is written for beginners and explains everything clearly, pointing you to the verses so you can read along.

faqs.question: Is this course only for Christians?
faqs.answer: Not at all. Seekers with honest questions are very welcome. The course explains who Jesus is and invites you to consider the good news.

faqs.question: Will I get a certificate?
faqs.answer: Yes. Complete all modules and pass the final assessment (70%) to earn your TIH Bible School certificate.

lessons.title: 1.1 The New Testament: The Story of Jesus and His Church
lessons.html:
The New Testament: The Story of Jesus and His Church

The New Testament is the second part of the Bible, 27 books written in the first century AD, mostly in Greek. If the Old Testament is the promise, the New Testament is the fulfillment. It announces the good news: the Savior God had promised for centuries has come, and His name is Jesus.

How the New Testament is arranged

  • The Gospels, Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John: four accounts of the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus.
  • Acts, the birth and growth of the early Church and the spread of the gospel.
  • The Letters (Epistles), 21 letters, many by Paul, teaching churches how to believe and live.
  • Revelation, a book of prophecy about Christ's victory and the end of the age.

The New Testament connects directly to the Old. It opens by presenting Jesus as the promised "son of David, the son of Abraham" (Matthew 1:1), showing that God kept every promise. As the book of Hebrews says, "in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son" (Hebrews 1:2).

As you survey the New Testament, keep asking: Who is Jesus? What has He done for us? And how then should we live as His people? These questions lead to the heart of the Christian faith.

lessons.title: 1.2 The Four Gospels: Four Portraits of Jesus
lessons.html:
The Four Gospels: Four Portraits of Jesus

The New Testament opens with four Gospels, Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. "Gospel" means "good news." Each is a true account of Jesus' life, but each was written for a different audience and highlights different aspects of who He is, like four portraits of the same person from four angles.

The distinct emphasis of each

  • Matthew, written especially for Jewish readers, presents Jesus as the promised Messiah and King, quoting many Old Testament prophecies.
  • Mark, the shortest, fast-paced Gospel, shows Jesus as the powerful Servant who acts and suffers for others.
  • Luke, written by a careful physician, presents Jesus as the compassionate Savior of all people, with special care for the poor, women, and outsiders.
  • John, the most theological, declares plainly that Jesus is God the Son: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God... and the Word became flesh" (John 1:1, 14).

Matthew, Mark, and Luke are called the "Synoptic" Gospels because they share a similar view and much overlapping material. John stands apart with unique conversations and signs. Together they give us a full, reliable picture of Jesus.

John explains why the Gospels were written: "these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name" (John 20:31). The Gospels are not neutral biographies, they are written to lead you to faith.

lessons.title: 1.3 The Birth and Early Life of Jesus
lessons.html:
The Birth and Early Life of Jesus

The Gospels of Matthew and Luke tell how the Son of God entered the world. Jesus was born in Bethlehem to the virgin Mary, exactly as the prophets had foretold (Micah 5:2; Isaiah 7:14). An angel announced His birth as good news of great joy, "for unto you is born this day... a Savior, who is Christ the Lord" (Luke 2:11).

The incarnation

This humble birth in a manger is one of the most staggering claims in all of Scripture: the eternal God became a human being. This is the incarnation, "the Word became flesh and dwelt among us" (John 1:14). God did not stay distant; He came near, sharing our humanity so He could rescue us.

Preparation for ministry

The Gospels tell us little about Jesus' childhood, except that He "increased in wisdom and in stature and in favor with God and man" (Luke 2:52). When He was about thirty, His public ministry began. John the Baptist, the messenger Malachi had promised, prepared the way, calling people to repent and baptizing Jesus in the Jordan River, where the Father spoke and the Spirit descended (Matthew 3).

Then Jesus was tempted by Satan in the wilderness for forty days but did not sin, answering each temptation with Scripture (Matthew 4:1-11). Having proven faithful where Israel had failed, He was ready to begin the ministry that would change the world.

lessons.title: 2.1 Jesus' Teaching: The Kingdom & Sermon on the Mount
lessons.html:
Jesus' Teaching: The Kingdom and the Sermon on the Mount

At the heart of Jesus' preaching was a single theme: the kingdom of God. "The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel" (Mark 1:15). The kingdom is God's reign, breaking into the world through Jesus and welcoming all who turn to Him.

The Sermon on the Mount

Jesus' most famous teaching is the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5-7). It turns the world's values upside down. It begins with the Beatitudes: "Blessed are the poor in spirit... Blessed are the meek... Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness" (Matthew 5:3-10). In God's kingdom, the humble and merciful are the truly blessed.

Jesus taught a righteousness of the heart, not just outward rule-keeping: not only "do not murder" but do not nurse hatred; not only "do not commit adultery" but guard your heart. He taught us to love even our enemies (Matthew 5:44), to give and pray sincerely, to store up "treasures in heaven" rather than on earth (Matthew 6:19-21), and to seek "first the kingdom of God" (Matthew 6:33).

The Golden Rule

He summed up much of the Law in one line: "whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them" (Matthew 7:12). Jesus' teaching is not a ladder to earn God's favor, but a portrait of the transformed life His people are called to live, a life only possible by His grace and Spirit.

lessons.title: 2.2 Parables and Miracles
lessons.html:
Parables and Miracles

Jesus taught in parables, short, vivid stories drawn from everyday life that revealed truth about God's kingdom. He also performed miracles that displayed His power and compassion and proved His identity as the Son of God.

The parables

Through parables, Jesus made deep truths memorable. The Prodigal Son (Luke 15) pictures a loving father who runs to welcome home a rebellious child, a portrait of God's grace toward sinners. The Good Samaritan (Luke 10) teaches us to love our neighbor, even across ethnic lines. The Sower (Mark 4) shows how people respond differently to God's Word. Each parable rewards those who truly want to understand.

The miracles

Jesus' miracles were not tricks but signs of the kingdom breaking in. He healed the sick, gave sight to the blind, and cleansed lepers. He showed power over nature by calming a storm (Mark 4:39) and feeding five thousand people with five loaves and two fish (John 6). He cast out demons, and He even raised the dead, most dramatically His friend Lazarus (John 11).

These signs revealed Jesus' compassion for hurting people and pointed to who He is. As Nicodemus admitted, "no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him" (John 3:2). The parables and miracles work together: the words explain the kingdom, and the works demonstrate its power.

lessons.title: 2.3 The Death and Resurrection of Jesus
lessons.html:
The Death and Resurrection of Jesus

Every Gospel builds toward its climax: the death and resurrection of Jesus. This is the center of the Christian faith and the fulfillment of God's plan to save the world.

The final week

Jesus entered Jerusalem to shouts of praise, shared a final Passover meal with His disciples (instituting the Lord's Supper), prayed in agony in the Garden of Gethsemane, and was betrayed by Judas and arrested. After unjust trials, He was condemned and crucified, a brutal Roman execution.

The meaning of the cross

Though it looked like defeat, the cross was God's plan of rescue. Jesus died as our substitute, bearing the punishment for sin: "he was pierced for our transgressions... and with his wounds we are healed" (Isaiah 53:5). His final words, "It is finished" (John 19:30), declared that the work of salvation was complete. The temple curtain tore in two, signaling that the way to God was now open.

The resurrection

On the third day, the tomb was empty. Jesus rose bodily from the dead and appeared to His disciples and to more than five hundred witnesses (1 Corinthians 15:3-6). The resurrection proves His victory over sin and death and confirms that He is the Son of God (Romans 1:4). Because He lives, all who trust Him will live also (John 14:19). This is the heartbeat of the good news.

modules.title: Module 3: Who Is Jesus & the Gospel

lessons.title: 3.1 Who Is Jesus? The Heart of the New Testament
lessons.html:
The Birth of the Church: Acts and Pentecost

The book of Acts, written by Luke, tells what happened after Jesus rose and returned to heaven. Before ascending, Jesus gave His followers a mission and a promise: "you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses... to the end of the earth" (Acts 1:8).

Pentecost

Fifty days after Passover, at the feast of Pentecost, the Holy Spirit was poured out on the believers just as Jesus promised (Acts 2). Filled with the Spirit, the once-fearful disciples boldly proclaimed the gospel. Peter preached, and about three thousand people believed and were baptized that day. The Church was born.

The early Church

The first believers "devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers" (Acts 2:42). They shared their possessions, cared for the needy, and worshiped joyfully. Despite arrests and opposition, "the Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved" (Acts 2:47).

The gospel spread outward exactly as Jesus said, first in Jerusalem, then Judea and Samaria, and finally toward the ends of the earth. Acts shows that the Church grows not by human cleverness but by the power of the Holy Spirit working through ordinary, faithful witnesses.

lessons.title: 3.2 The Gospel Message and How to Respond
lessons.html:
The Gospel Spreads: Persecution and Mission

As the Church grew, so did opposition. The book of Acts records both fierce persecution and unstoppable mission, and shows how God used even suffering to spread the good news.

Stephen and scattering

Stephen became the first Christian martyr, stoned for his bold witness while praying for his killers (Acts 7). The persecution that followed scattered believers throughout the region, but everywhere they went, they preached the gospel (Acts 8:4). What enemies meant for harm, God used to spread His message.

The conversion of Saul

One of the fiercest persecutors was Saul of Tarsus. On the road to Damascus, the risen Jesus met him in blinding light, and Saul was transformed (Acts 9). Renamed Paul, he became the greatest missionary in history, carrying the gospel across the Roman world. His dramatic conversion shows that no one is beyond the reach of God's grace.

The gospel for all nations

A turning point came when God showed Peter that the good news is for everyone, not only the Jews (Acts 10). Gentiles (non-Jews) received the Holy Spirit and were welcomed into the Church. Paul then made several missionary journeys, planting churches across Asia Minor and Europe, always taking the gospel to new peoples. The message that began in Jerusalem was reaching the whole world, and one day it would reach Liberia and you.

lessons.title: 3.3 The Reliability of the New Testament
lessons.html:
Paul's Letters to the Churches

As Paul planted churches, he wrote letters (epistles) to teach, correct, and encourage them. Thirteen New Testament letters bear his name, and they form much of the Christian teaching we rely on today. They were real letters to real congregations facing real questions.

The great themes of Paul's letters

  • Romans, Paul's masterpiece explaining the gospel: all have sinned, but we are "justified by faith" in Christ (Romans 3:23; 5:1), and "there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus" (Romans 8:1).
  • 1 & 2 Corinthians, practical guidance for a struggling church on unity, love (1 Corinthians 13), and the resurrection.
  • Galatians, a passionate defense that we are saved by grace through faith, not by keeping the law.
  • Ephesians & Philippians, the riches of our salvation and joy in Christ: "For by grace you have been saved through faith" (Ephesians 2:8); "I can do all things through him who strengthens me" (Philippians 4:13).

Paul's letters usually follow a pattern: first the truth of what God has done for us in Christ, then the response, how we should therefore live. This is the gospel logic: because of God's grace (indicative), live a transformed life (imperative). We do not obey to be saved; we obey because we are saved.

lessons.title: 🛠️ Project: Share the Story of Jesus
lessons.html: Module 3 Project, Share the Story of Jesus. In 150–300 words, explain the good news of Jesus as if to a friend who has never heard it. Include four parts: who Jesus is, why He came, what happened at the cross and the empty tomb, and how a person can respond. Use at least two Bible verses from this module. This exercise helps you internalize the gospel and prepares you to share it with others, the very purpose of the New Testament.

modules.title: Module 4: The Early Church and Paul

lessons.title: 4.1 The Birth of the Church: Acts and Pentecost
lessons.html:
Living the Christian Life: The General Letters

Beyond Paul's letters, the New Testament includes letters from other leaders, often called the General Letters, including Hebrews, James, 1 and 2 Peter, the letters of John, and Jude. They give practical wisdom for living out the faith, especially under pressure.

Faith that works and endures

  • Hebrews shows that Jesus is greater than everything in the Old Testament, a better priest offering a better sacrifice, and calls us to persevere in faith (Hebrews 12:1-2).
  • James insists that genuine faith produces action: "faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead" (James 2:17). He gives practical teaching on the tongue, wisdom, and caring for the needy.
  • 1 Peter encourages believers suffering for their faith to stand firm, following Christ's example of suffering.
  • 1 John assures believers of eternal life and stresses that those who know God will love one another: "God is love" (1 John 4:8).

These letters remind us that Christianity is not just something we believe but something we live. Real faith shows itself in love, integrity, endurance, and holiness, especially when following Jesus is costly. They are deeply practical, addressing money, speech, relationships, suffering, and false teaching.

For believers in every generation and place, the General Letters offer steady encouragement: hold fast to Christ, love one another, do what is right, and keep going, for the reward is sure.

lessons.title: 4.2 The Gospel Spreads: Persecution and Mission
lessons.html:
The Church as God's Family and Body

The New Testament uses rich pictures to describe the Church, the community of all who belong to Jesus. Understanding these images shapes how we live together as Christians.

Three pictures of the Church

  • The Body of Christ, "you are the body of Christ and individually members of it" (1 Corinthians 12:27). Just as a body has many parts with different functions, the Church has many members with different gifts, all needed and all working together under Christ the head.
  • The Family of God, believers are brothers and sisters, adopted as God's children (Ephesians 2:19). The Church is not an organization we join but a family we are born into.
  • The Temple of the Spirit, together believers are "a holy temple in the Lord," where God dwells by His Spirit (Ephesians 2:21-22).

Life together

Because we belong to one another, the New Testament is full of "one another" commands: love one another, encourage one another, bear one another's burdens (Galatians 6:2), forgive one another. Every believer has a spiritual gift to serve the whole (1 Corinthians 12:7), whether teaching, serving, giving, or showing mercy.

The Church is meant to display God's love to the world. Jesus said, "By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another" (John 13:35). A healthy church is not perfect, but it is a family growing together in love and truth.

lessons.title: 4.3 Paul's Letters to the Churches
lessons.html:
Hope and Victory: The Book of Revelation

The final book of the Bible, Revelation, was given to the apostle John while exiled on the island of Patmos. It is a book of prophecy full of vivid symbols and visions, written to encourage persecuted Christians with a powerful message: Jesus wins.

What Revelation is about

Though its imagery can seem strange, Revelation's main point is clear. It pulls back the curtain to show the risen, glorified Christ reigning over history (Revelation 1). It warns and encourages seven real churches, portrays the cosmic conflict between good and evil, and assures believers that God is in control even when evil seems to triumph.

The glorious ending

Revelation ends with the most beautiful promise in Scripture. Jesus returns in victory, evil is finally defeated, and God makes all things new: "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man... He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain" (Revelation 21:3-4). A new heaven and new earth become the eternal home of God's people.

The Bible closes with a longing and a promise: Jesus says, "Surely I am coming soon," and the Church answers, "Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!" (Revelation 22:20). Revelation gives suffering believers courage: however dark the present, the final chapter is certain, and it is glorious. Christ reigns, and His people will reign with Him forever.

lessons.title: 5.1 Living the Christian Life: The General Letters
lessons.html:
The Whole Story: How the Bible Fits Together

Having surveyed the New Testament, step back to see how the entire Bible forms one story in four great movements. Understanding this "big picture" transforms how you read every individual passage.

Creation, Fall, Redemption, Restoration

  1. Creation, God made a good world and placed humanity in it to know and serve Him (Genesis 1-2).
  2. Fall, humanity rebelled, bringing sin, death, and brokenness into everything (Genesis 3).
  3. Redemption, God launched a rescue plan, promising a Savior through Israel and fulfilling it in the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus (Luke 24:27).
  4. Restoration, God is gathering a people (the Church) and will one day make all things new (Revelation 21).

The New Testament sits at the hinge of this story. Everything the Old Testament promised, a Savior, a new covenant, God's Spirit poured out, blessing for all nations, comes true in Jesus. "For all the promises of God find their Yes in him" (2 Corinthians 1:20).

This is why the Bible, though written by many authors over 1,500 years, is one unified book. It has one Author (God), one hero (Jesus), and one message (God saving a people for Himself). When you read any part, ask how it fits this grand story, and you will read with new understanding and wonder.

lessons.title: 5.2 The Church as God's Family and Body
lessons.html:
Applying the New Testament to Your Life

The New Testament was never meant to be only studied, it is meant to be lived. James warns against being "hearers only," urging us to be "doers of the word" (James 1:22). This lesson helps you turn what you have learned into a transformed life.

From knowledge to obedience

As you read the New Testament, look for four things in each passage: a promise to trust, a command to obey, a sin to avoid, and an example to follow. Then respond in prayer and action. Truth becomes transformation when we do what God says.

The shape of a New Testament life

  • Love God wholeheartedly and love your neighbor as yourself (Matthew 22:37-39), the summary of it all.
  • Grow in Christ through Scripture, prayer, and the fellowship of the church.
  • Serve others with the gifts God has given you, following Jesus who "came not to be served but to serve" (Mark 10:45).
  • Witness to the good news wherever you are, with your words and your changed life.

Remember the gospel logic that runs through every letter: we do not obey in order to be accepted; we obey because in Christ we already are. Our motivation is grateful love: "We love because he first loved us" (1 John 4:19).

lessons.title: 5.3 Hope and Victory: The Book of Revelation
lessons.html:
Continuing to Grow: Your Next Steps

Congratulations, you have surveyed the entire New Testament, from the Gospels through Acts, the letters, and Revelation. But a survey is only the beginning. Jesus calls His people to keep "growing in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ" (2 Peter 3:18) for a lifetime.

A plan for lifelong growth

  1. Read the Gospels deeply. Return often to Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John to know Jesus better, the whole point of the New Testament.
  2. Study one letter at a time. Read a short book like Philippians or 1 John slowly, asking how to live it out.
  3. Pray the Scriptures. Turn what you read into conversation with God.
  4. Join God's family. Commit to a Bible-believing local church for worship, teaching, and fellowship (Hebrews 10:25).
  5. Obey and serve. Put truth into practice and use your gifts to bless others.
  6. Share the good news. Tell others about the Jesus you are coming to know.

The God who inspired these Scriptures wants to use them to change your life. "All Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching... that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work" (2 Timothy 3:16-17).

Consider completing your Bible School studies with the Old Testament Survey and Christian Foundations & Discipleship courses. Keep walking with Jesus, the best is yet to come. "He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion" (Philippians 1:6).

modules.title: Module 6: The Whole Story & Next Steps

lessons.title: 6.1 The Whole Story: How the Bible Fits Together
lessons.html:
Who Is Jesus? The Heart of the New Testament

Everything in the New Testament centers on one question that Jesus Himself asked His disciples: "Who do you say that I am?" (Matthew 16:15). How you answer this question shapes your whole life and eternity. This lesson gathers the New Testament's clear answer.

The New Testament's claims about Jesus

  • He is God the Son, "the Word was God... became flesh" (John 1:1, 14); He accepted worship and forgave sins.
  • He is the promised Messiah, the Christ, the fulfillment of the Old Testament hope (Matthew 1:1).
  • He is the only Savior, "there is salvation in no one else" (Acts 4:12); "no one comes to the Father except through me" (John 14:6).
  • He is the risen, reigning Lord, raised from death and given "the name that is above every name" (Philippians 2:9-11).

Why it matters

Jesus is not merely a good teacher or prophet among many. The New Testament presents Him as God who became man to save us, died in our place, rose in victory, and now reigns as Lord of all. To know Him is to have eternal life (John 17:3).

Peter answered Jesus' question rightly: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God" (Matthew 16:16). The New Testament invites you to make the same confession, not just with your lips, but with your whole heart and life. Everything else in the Christian faith flows from getting Jesus right.

lessons.title: 6.2 Applying the New Testament to Your Life
lessons.html:
The Gospel Message and How to Respond

The New Testament exists to announce and explain one message: the gospel, the good news of salvation through Jesus Christ. Having surveyed the whole New Testament, it is worth stating this message clearly and simply, because it is meant not just to be understood, but to be received.

The gospel in four movements

  1. God, the holy, loving Creator made us for relationship with Him (John 3:16).
  2. Sin, we have all rebelled against God, and sin separates us from Him (Romans 3:23; 6:23).
  3. Jesus, God the Son became man, lived sinlessly, died for our sins, and rose again (1 Corinthians 15:3-4).
  4. Response, we are saved by turning from sin (repentance) and trusting in Jesus (faith) (Romans 10:9).

How to respond today

Salvation is a free gift received by faith, not earned by works: "For by grace you have been saved through faith... it is the gift of God" (Ephesians 2:8-9). To receive it, you simply come to Jesus, admitting your need, believing He died and rose for you, and trusting Him as Savior and Lord. "Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life" (John 3:36).

If you have never done so, you can respond right now with a simple, honest prayer: thank Jesus for dying for you, ask His forgiveness, and give Him your life. And if you already belong to Him, let this good news fill you with joy and send you out to share it, for the whole New Testament is, at its heart, an invitation to know and follow Jesus.

lessons.title: 6.3 Continuing to Grow: Your Next Steps
lessons.html:
The Reliability of the New Testament

Can we trust the New Testament? This is an important question, and the New Testament itself invites investigation. Luke says he "carefully investigated everything" and wrote "an orderly account" so we may have "certainty" (Luke 1:3-4). Christianity rests not on myths but on real events witnessed by real people.

Reasons for confidence

  • Eyewitness testimony. The Gospels and letters were written within decades of the events, by or from eyewitnesses. Paul points to more than 500 people who saw the risen Jesus, "most of whom are still alive" (1 Corinthians 15:6), inviting readers to check.
  • Manuscript evidence. The New Testament is preserved in thousands of ancient manuscripts, far more than any other ancient text, allowing us to know its original wording with great confidence.
  • Honest reporting. The writers recorded their own failures and included details (like women as the first witnesses of the resurrection) that no one would invent, a mark of truthful testimony.
  • Transformed lives. The disciples were willing to suffer and die for their claim that Jesus rose, people do not die for what they know to be a lie.

Of course, faith is more than intellectual proof; it is trust in a Person. But that trust is reasonable. The New Testament stands on solid historical ground, and the God who inspired it uses it to bring people to living faith. As Jesus said, "you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free" (John 8:32).

questions.explanation: The New Testament has 27 books.

questions.question: Jesus was born in Bethlehem to:
questions.explanation: Jesus was born to the virgin Mary in Bethlehem.

questions.question: The central theme of Jesus' preaching was:
questions.explanation: Jesus preached the kingdom of God (Mark 1:15).

questions.question: The Sermon on the Mount begins with the:
questions.explanation: Matthew 5 opens with the Beatitudes.

questions.question: Jesus taught mainly through short stories called:
questions.explanation: Parables reveal truths about God's kingdom.

questions.question: On the cross Jesus died as:
questions.explanation: Jesus bore our sins as our substitute (Isaiah 53:5).

questions.question: "It is finished" declared that:
questions.explanation: John 19:30, the work of salvation was accomplished.

questions.question: The resurrection of Jesus:
questions.explanation: Jesus rose bodily, proving His victory over death.

questions.question: The Holy Spirit came upon the believers at:
questions.explanation: The Spirit was poured out at Pentecost (Acts 2).

questions.question: The persecutor who became the great missionary Paul was named:
questions.explanation: Saul of Tarsus became Paul after meeting the risen Jesus.

options: To the end of the earth

questions.question: Romans teaches that we are:

questions.question: "For by grace you have been saved through faith" is in:
questions.explanation: Ephesians 2:8-9, salvation by grace through faith.

questions.question: James teaches that genuine faith:
questions.explanation: Real faith produces works (James 2:17).

questions.question: The Church is pictured in the New Testament as:
options: The body and family of Christ

questions.question: Revelation's main message is that:
questions.explanation: Revelation assures believers that Christ wins.

questions.question: The whole Bible tells one story often summarized as:
questions.explanation: The Bible's storyline: Creation, Fall, Redemption, Restoration.
